explanation: Endothermic animals with feathers, pneumatic pneumatic (hollow) bones, and crop/gizzard.

bullets: O – Oviparous (Egg-laying) mammal
O – Ornithorhynchus (Platypus)
explanation: Rare egg-laying mammal species despite possessing mammary glands.

mnemonic: Macropus Pteropus Camelus Macaca Rattus Canis Felis Elephas Equus Delphinus Balaenoptera Panthera
bullets: Macropus (Kangaroo), Pteropus (Flying fox), Camelus (Camel)
Macaca (Monkey), Rattus (Rat), Canis (Dog), Felis (Cat)
Elephas (Elephant), Equus (Horse), Delphinus (Dolphin), Balaenoptera (Blue whale), Panthera (Tiger/Lion)
explanation: Mammalian species giving birth to live young, featuring hair and external ears (pinnae).

bullets: 2 Chambers (1A, 1V): Fishes
3 Chambers (2A, 1V): Amphibians, Reptiles (except crocodile)
4 Chambers (2A, 2V): Crocodilians, Birds, Mammals
explanation: Evolutionary progression of heart septation and circulatory pathways.

mnemonic: Warm: Birds & Mammals | Cold: Rest (Fish, Amphibia, Reptilia)
bullets: Homeotherms: Maintain constant body temp (Aves, Mammalia)
Poikilotherms: Body temp varies with environment (Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia)
explanation: Thermoregulation capacity differences across vertebrate taxonomic classes. Chapter 4: Animal Kingdom (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

topic: Regions of Root Tip (Proximal to Distal)
bullets: Region of Maturation (Root hairs present)
Region of Elongation (Responsible for growth in length)
Region of Meristematic Activity (Rapidly dividing small cells)
Root Cap (Thimble-like protective structure at apex)
explanation: Anatomical zones of a root tip ordered from base/proximal side to apex/distal tip.

topic: Tap Root System vs Fibrous Root System
mnemonic: Dicot Tap Mustard, Monocot Fibrous Wheat
bullets: Tap Root: Dicots (Primary root directly elongates from radicle, e.g., Mustard)
Fibrous Root: Monocots (Primary root short-lived, replaced by roots from stem base, e.g., Wheat)
explanation: Major root origin differences distinguishing dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous plants.

bullets: G – Grass
M – Monstera
B – Banyan tree
explanation: Roots arising from parts of the plant other than the radicle.

bullets: Prop Roots: Hanging supportive roots in Banyan tree
Stilt Roots: Supporting roots coming out of lower stem nodes in Maize and Sugarcane
explanation: Mechanical support root adaptations arising aerial stem parts.

bullets: R – Rhizophora (Grows in swampy areas)
P – Pneumatophores (Grow vertically upwards to get oxygen for respiration)
explanation: Negatively geotropic specialized roots in halophytes aiding gas exchange.

bullets: P – Potato (Tuber)
T – Ginger (Rhizome)
Z – Zaminkand (Corm)
G – Garlic / Onion (Bulb)
C – Colocasia (Corm)
explanation: Underground stem modifications adapted for perennation and food storage. Chapter 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

topic: Stem Modifications for Climbing and Defense
mnemonic: Tendrils Gourd Grape, Thorns Citrus Bougainvillea
bullets: Stem Tendrils (Climbing): Cucumber, Pumpkins, Watermelon (Gourds), Grapevines
Stem Thorns (Defense): Citrus, Bougainvillea
explanation: Axillary buds modifying into slender spirally coiled tendrils or woody straight sharp thorns.

mnemonic: Runner Grass Strawberry, Offset Pistia Eichhornia, Sucker Banana Pineapple
bullets: Runner: Grass, Strawberry
Offset: Pistia, Eichhornia (Water Hyacinth)
Sucker: Banana, Pineapple, Chrysanthemum
explanation: Vegetative propagation stem adaptations spreading laterally to colonize new niches.

bullets: Flattened stem: Opuntia
Cylindrical stem: Euphorbia
explanation: Arid zone stem modifications taking over photosynthetic function while leaves form spines.

bullets: Reticulate Venation: Network of veinlets (Dicots)
Parallel Venation: Veins run parallel within lamina (Monocots)
explanation: Leaf vein arrangement patterns characteristic of two main angiosperm classes.

bullets: Pinnately Compound: Leaflets on common axis/rachis (e.g., Neem)
Palmately Compound: Leaflets attached at common point/petiole tip (e.g., Silk Cotton)
explanation: Leaf blade incision types reaching up to the midrib or petiole top.

mnemonic: Alternate Mustard China Sunflower, Opposite Calotropis Guava, Whorled Alstonia
bullets: Alternate: Single leaf per node (Mustard, China rose, Sunflower)
Opposite: Pair of leaves per node (Calotropis, Guava)
Whorled: More than two leaves per node (Alstonia)
explanation: Pattern of leaf arrangement on stem or branch nodes. Chapter 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

mnemonic: Racemose Indefinite Acropetal, Cymose Definite Basipetal
bullets: Racemose: Main axis continues to grow; flowers borne in acropetal succession
Cymose: Main axis terminates in flower; flowers borne in basipetal order
explanation: Flower arrangement patterns on floral axis based on terminal growth capability.

mnemonic: Actino Mustard Datura Chilli, Zygo Pea Gulmohur Bean Cassia, Asym Canna
bullets: Actinomorphic (Radial): Mustard, Datura, Chilli
Zygomorphic (Bilateral): Pea, Gulmohur, Bean, Cassia
Asymmetric (Irregular): Canna
explanation: Floral symmetry division planes passing through the central floral axis.

topic: Position of Floral Parts on Thalamus
mnemonic: Hypo Mustard China Brinjal, Peri Plum Rose Peach, Epi Guava Cucumber Ray-Floret
bullets: Hypogynous (Superior Ovary): Mustard, China rose, Brinjal
Perigynous (Half-Inferior Ovary): Plum, Rose, Peach
Epigynous (Inferior Ovary): Guava, Cucumber, Ray florets of Sunflower
explanation: Relative positional arrangement of calyx, corolla, and androecium with respect to ovary.

mnemonic: Valvate Calotropis, Twisted China Lady Cotton, Imbricate Cassia Gulmohur, Vexillary Pea Bean
bullets: Valvate: Calotropis
Twisted: China rose, Lady's finger, Cotton
Imbricate: Cassia, Gulmohur
Vexillary (Papilionaceous): Pea, Bean
explanation: Overlapping pattern of floral whorl components in bud stage prior to opening.

bullets: Standard (Banner): 1 large outer petal
Wings (Alae): 2 lateral petals
Keel (Carina): 2 smallest anterior fused petals
explanation: Papilionaceous corolla layout composed of 5 distinct petals (1+2+(2)).

mnemonic: Mono China, Di Pea, Poly Citrus
bullets: Monadelphous (Fused into 1 bundle): China rose
Diadelphous (Fused into 2 bundles): Pea (9+1 arrangement)
Polyadelphous (Fused into >2 bundles): Citrus
explanation: Cohesion of stamen filaments forming unified groups or bundles. Chapter 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

bullets: Salvia
Mustard
explanation: Genera exhibiting variable length among stamens within the same individual flower.

bullets: Epipetalous: Stamens attached to petals (e.g., Brinjal)
Epiphyllous (Epitepalous): Stamens attached to perianth/tepals (e.g., Lily)
explanation: Adhesion of stamen filaments to non-androecial floral whorls.

mnemonic: Marginal Pea, Axile China Tomato Lemon, Parietal Mustard Argemone, Free-Central Dianthus Primrose, Basal Sunflower Marigold
bullets: Marginal: Pea
Axile: China rose, Tomato, Lemon
Parietal: Mustard, Argemone
Free-Central: Dianthus, Primrose
Basal: Sunflower, Marigold
explanation: Pattern of ovule attachment along placenta inside the ovary walls.

bullets: Mango: Fleshy edible mesocarp, hard stony endocarp
Coconut: Fibrous mesocarp (coir source)
explanation: Monocarpellary superior ovary fruits characterized by a stony endocarp.

topic: Seed Structure: Endospermic vs Non-Endospermic Seeds
mnemonic: Endo Castor Monocots, Non-Endo Pea Gram Bean
bullets: Endospermic (Albuminous): Castor (dicot!), Maize, Wheat, Barley
Non-Endospermic (Exalbuminous): Pea, Gram, Bean, Orchid (monocot!)
explanation: Retention or complete consumption of endosperm tissue during embryo development.

bullets: Aleurone Layer: Proteinaceous outer layer of endosperm
Scutellum: Single large shield-shaped cotyledon
Coleoptile: Protective sheath covering plumule
Coleorhiza: Protective sheath covering radicle
explanation: Specialized morphological anatomical parts of a monocotyledonous grain. Chapter 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

bullets: Calyx: 5 sepals gamosepalous, imbricate
Corolla: 5 petals polypetalous, vexillary aestivation
Androecium: Diadelphous (9)+1
Gynoecium: Superior, monocarpellary, marginal placentation
explanation: Key diagnostic floral characters of legume family (Fabaceae).

mnemonic: Pulses Edible-Oil Dye Fibres Fodder Ornamentals Medicine
bullets: Pulses: Gram, Arhar, Sem, Moong, Soyabean
Edible Oil: Soyabean, Groundnut | Dye: Indigofera
Fibres: Sunhemp | Fodder: Sesbania, Trifolium
Ornamentals: Lupin, Sweet pea | Medicine: Muliathi
explanation: NCERT economic importance species catalog for Fabaceae.

bullets: Flower: ⊕ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2)
Calyx: Persistent sepals with valvate aestivation
Corolla: Gamopetalous with valvate aestivation
Androecium: 5 stamens, epipetalous
Gynoecium: Bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary, axile placentation with swollen placenta
explanation: Key diagnostic floral characters of potato family (Solanaceae).

bullets: Food: Tomato, Brinjal, Potato
Spice: Chilli | Fumigatory: Tobacco
Medicine: Belladonna, Ashwagandha
Ornamental: Petunia
explanation: NCERT economic importance species catalog for Solanaceae.

bullets: Flower: ⊕ P(3+3) A3+3 G(3)
Perianth: Tepals 6 (3+3), often united into tube
Androecium: Stamens 6 (3+3), epiphyllous
Gynoecium: Tricarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary, axile placentation
explanation: Key diagnostic floral features of monocot lily family (Liliaceae).

bullets: Ornamentals: Tulip, Gloriosa
Medicine: Aloe
Vegetables: Asparagus
Colchicine Source: Colchicum autumnale
explanation: NCERT economic importance species catalog for Liliaceae. Chapter 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

bullets: Apical Meristem: Primary growth at root and shoot tips
Intercalary Meristem: Between mature tissues (e.g., grasses)
Lateral Meristem: Secondary growth in thickness/girth
explanation: Primary meristems (Apical & Intercalary) increase length; lateral meristems increase thickness.

bullets: Primary Meristems: Appear early in life, build primary plant body
Secondary (Lateral) Meristems: Appear later, e.g., Fascicular cambium, Cork cambium
explanation: Primary meristems contribute to longitudinal growth; lateral meristems drive secondary thickening.

bullets: Parenchyma: Thin-walled, living, major organ filler
Collenchyma: Pectin-thickened corners, flexible support in young stems
Sclerenchyma: Dead cells, lignified, rigid strength
explanation: Tissues made of one cell type performing structural, storage, or mechanical roles.

bullets: Pectin: Wall localized thick corners (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin)
Petiole: Provides mechanical support to young dicot stems and petioles
explanation: Living mechanical tissue lacking intercellular spaces; absent in monocots.

bullets: Fibers: Elongated, pointed ends, thick lignified walls
Sclereids: Spherical/cylindrical with narrow lumen (e.g., pulp of pear, sapota)
explanation: Highly lignified dead elements providing rigidity to seed coats and fruit walls.

bullets: Xylem: Conducts water and mineral salts unidirectionally
Phloem: Conducts organic food solutes bidirectionally
explanation: Vascular complex tissues containing more than one cell type working as a unit. Chapter 6: Anatomy of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

mnemonic: T V F P” (Tracheids, Vessels, Fibers, Parenchyma)
bullets: Tracheids: Elongated dead cells with lignified walls
Vessels: Tube-like syncytial structures with perforated end plates
Xylem Fibers: Highly thickened walls with obliterated lumens
Xylem Parenchyma: Living cells storing food and water
explanation: Xylem parenchyma is the only living component among the four xylem elements.

bullets: Gymnosperms: Conduct water mainly via tracheids
Angiosperms: Possess true xylem vessels as a key diagnostic feature
explanation: Presence of vessels is a hallmark characteristic of angiospermic xylem.

topic: Primary Xylem Types: Protoxylem vs Metaxylem
mnemonic: Stem Endarch (Protoxylem Inside), Root Exarch (Protoxylem Outside)
bullets: Endarch (Stems): Protoxylem towards center (pith), Metaxylem towards periphery
Exarch (Roots): Protoxylem towards periphery, Metaxylem towards center
explanation: Directional maturation arrangement of first-formed xylem (protoxylem) relative to center.

mnemonic: S C F P” (Sieve tube, Companion cell, Fibers, Parenchyma)
bullets: Sieve Tube Elements: Enucleated living conducting cells
Companion Cells: Parenchymatous cells maintaining sieve element pressure
Phloem Fibers (Bast Fibers): Dead mechanical fibers (e.g., Jute, Flax, Hemp)
Phloem Parenchyma: Living storage cells absent in most monocots
explanation: Phloem fibers are the only non-living element in primary and secondary phloem.

mnemonic: Gymno Lacks Sieve Tubes & Companion Cells
bullets: Albuminous Cells: Replace companion cells in gymnosperms
Sieve Cells: Replace organized sieve tube elements
explanation: Gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells instead of sieve tube companion cell complexes.

bullets: Epidermal: Epidermis, Stomata, Trichomes, Root hairs
Ground (Fundemental): Cortex, Pericycle, Pith, Mesophyll
Vascular: Xylem and Phloem bundles
explanation: Three major structural tissue systems based on position and function in the plant body. Chapter 6: Anatomy of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

bullets: Stomatal Pore: Central aperture for gas exchange
Guard Cells: Kidney/Dumbbell-shaped cells regulating aperture
Subsidiary Cells: Specialized epidermal cells surrounding guard cells
explanation: Together, pore, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells form the stomatal apparatus.

topic: Guard Cell Shape in Grasses vs Dicots
bullets: Monocots (Grasses): Dumbbell-shaped guard cells
Dicots: Bean/Kidney-shaped guard cells
explanation: Guard cell shape variation dictates stomatal movement mechanics across classes.

topic: Epidermal Appendages: Root Hairs vs Trichomes
mnemonic: Root Unicellular Unbranched, Stem Multicellular Branched
bullets: Root Hairs: Unicellular elongations absorbing water
Trichomes: Multicellular shoot hairs preventing water loss
explanation: Structural differences and functional roles of root vs shoot epidermal outgrowths.

topic: Vascular Bundle Types: Radial vs Conjoint
bullets: Radial: Xylem and Phloem arranged in alternate radii (Roots)
Conjoint: Xylem and Phloem present along same radius (Stems & Leaves)
explanation: Spatial orientation arrangement of vascular tissues in organ cross-sections.

mnemonic: Open Dicot Cambium, Closed Monocot No-Cambium
bullets: Open Bundle: Intrafascicular cambium present between xylem and phloem (Dicots)
Closed Bundle: Cambium absent, no secondary growth potential (Monocots)
explanation: Presence of vascular cambium determines secondary growth capability.

mnemonic: Epiblema Cortex Endodermis Pericycle Xylem Pith
bullets: Epiblema: Outer layer with root hairs
Endodermis: Single layer with Casparian strips (suberin)
Pericycle: Gives rise to lateral roots and vascular cambium
Xylem condition: Diarch to tetrarch, exarch
explanation: Concentric anatomical layout of dicot roots from outer surface to center. Chapter 6: Anatomy of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

topic: Dicot Root vs Monocot Root (Pith & Xylem Bundles)
bullets: Dicot Root: Small/inconspicuous pith, 2–4 (diarch to tetrarch) xylem bundles
Monocot Root: Large well-developed pith, >6 (polyarch) xylem bundles
explanation: Critical distinguishing features between dicot and monocot root cross-sections.

bullets: Ring Layout: Vascular bundles in a characteristic ring
Bundle Type: Conjoint, open with cambium
Xylem: Endarch protoxylem
Hypodermis: Collenchymatous
explanation: Structural hallmark of dicotyledonous stem internal layout.

bullets: Scattered Bundles: Conjoint, closed vascular bundles
Hypodermis: Sclerenchymatous
Bundle Sheath: Sclerenchymatous surrounding sheath
Water Cavity: Lysigenous water cavity present in xylem
explanation: Distinct features of monocot stems with no secondary growth.

bullets: Palisade Parenchyma: Elongated, vertically arranged on adaxial (upper) side
Spongy Parenchyma: Loose oval cells with air cavities on abaxial (lower) side
explanation: Differentiated mesophyll organization characteristic of dorsiventral leaves.

mnemonic: Isobilateral Equal Stomata, Bulliform Roll Leaf
bullets: Isobilateral: Stomata on both surfaces, undifferentiated mesophyll
Bulliform Cells: Large, empty, colorless epidermal cells in grasses that roll leaves to prevent water loss
explanation: Adaptation in monocot leaves to reduce transpiration during water stress.

bullets: Intrafascicular Cambium: Present inside primary vascular bundle
Interfascicular Cambium: Forms from medullary ray cells between bundles
explanation: Medullary rays dedifferentiate to join intrafascicular cambium, completing the ring. Chapter 6: Anatomy of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

mnemonic: Inside Secondary Xylem, Outside Secondary Phloem
bullets: Secondary Xylem (Wood): Cut off towards inside/pith (produced in larger quantity)
Secondary Phloem: Cut off towards outside/periphery
explanation: Cambium is more active on the inner side, accumulating thick secondary xylem layers.

mnemonic: Spring Early Light Low-Density, Autumn Late Dark High-Density
bullets: Spring Wood (Early Wood): Wide vessels, lighter color, lower density
Autumn Wood (Late Wood): Narrow vessels, darker color, higher density
explanation: Seasonal cambial activity forming concentric annual rings used in dendrochronology.

mnemonic: Heart Central Dark Dead Non-Conducting, Sap Outer Light Living Conducting
bullets: Heartwood (Duramen): Central region, dark, highly lignified with organic deposits, non-conducting, resistant to pests
Sapwood (Alburnum): Peripheral region, lighter, active in water and mineral conduction
explanation: Aging secondary xylem functional differentiation in older woody trees.

bullets: Phellogen: Cork cambium (meristematic layer)
Phellem: Cork cells (suberin-deposited, dead) towards outside
Phelloderm: Secondary cortex (parenchymatous) towards inside
explanation: Secondary protective tissue replacing broken epidermis during girth growth.

bullets: Early Bark (Soft Bark): Formed early in the season
Late Bark (Hard Bark): Formed towards end of season
Constituents: Periderm + Secondary Phloem
explanation: Non-technical term for all tissues exterior to the vascular cambial ring.

bullets: Structure: Lens-shaped openings in bark formed by loose complementary cells
Function: Permit gaseous exchange between internal stem tissues and atmosphere
explanation: Ruptured periderm areas allowing aeration in secondary thickened woody stems. Chapter 6: Anatomy of Flowering Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

mnemonic: E C M N” (Epithelial, Connective, Muscular, Nervous)
bullets: Epithelial: Covering/lining tissue with tightly packed cells
Connective: Most abundant, binds and supports other tissues
Muscular: Contractile tissue responsible for movements
Nervous: Excitable tissue controlling body responsiveness
explanation: The four basic tissue types constituting all complex animal organ systems.

bullets: A – Alveoli of lungs (diffusion boundary)
B – Blood vessels (endothelium)
L – Lymphatic vessels
E – Excretory bowman's capsule (filtration membrane)
explanation: Single layer of flattened cells with irregular boundaries adapted for filtration and diffusion.

bullets: D – Ducts of glands (salivary, pancreatic)
N – Nephron tubular parts (secretion and absorption)
G – Germinal epithelium of ovaries/testes
P – PCT of nephron (bears microvilli)
explanation: Single layer of cube-like cells primarily performing secretory and absorptive functions.

bullets: S – Stomach lining
I – Intestine lining (has microvilli for absorption)
G – Gallbladder lining
explanation: Tall column-like cells with basal nuclei involved in secretion and absorption across gastrointestinal tract.

mnemonic: B F C” (Bronchioles, Fallopian tubes, Cilia)
bullets: B – Bronchioles (moves mucus outwards)
F – Fallopian tubes (moves ovum towards uterus)
C – Ciliated columnar/cuboidal structure
explanation: Epithelium bearing cilia on free surface to propel particles or fluids in a specific direction.

bullets: Tight Junctions: Stop substances from leaking across tissue
Adhering Junctions: Perform cementing to keep neighboring cells together
Gap Junctions: Facilitate intercellular communication by connecting cytoplasm
explanation: Specialized structural junctions providing physical connection and communication between epithelial cells. Chapter 7: Structural Organisation in Animals (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

bullets: Areolar Tissue: Serves as support framework for epithelium under skin; contains fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells
Adipose Tissue: Fat-storing tissue located mainly beneath the skin
explanation: Connective tissues with cells and fibers loosely arranged in a semi-fluid ground substance.

topic: Dense Connective Tissue: Tendon vs Ligament
mnemonic: T M B, L B B
bullets: T M B: Tendon connects Muscle to Bone
L B B: Ligament connects Bone to Bone
explanation: Dense regular connective tissues where collagen fibers run in parallel bundles to withstand tension.

bullets: Cartilage: Solid, pliable matrix; chondrocytes in lacunae
Bone: Hard, non-pliable matrix rich in calcium salts and collagen; osteocytes
Blood: Fluid connective tissue with plasma, RBCs, WBCs, and platelets
explanation: Specialized supportive and transport tissues lacking structural fibers in blood.

bullets: Skeletal: Striated, voluntary, multinucleated, unbranched
Smooth: Non-striated (visceral), involuntary, spindle-shaped (fusiform), uninucleated
Cardiac: Striated, involuntary, branched, intercalated discs present
explanation: Three muscle categories based on cross-striations, control mechanisms, and cellular morphology.

bullets: Intercalated Discs: Unique cellular communication junctions in cardiac muscle
Function: Allows cardiac cells to contract as a single unit (functional syncytium)
explanation: Plasma membrane fusion points in heart muscle allowing rapid electrical signal impulse spread.

bullets: Neurons: Excitable structural units that transmit electrical impulses
Neuroglial Cells: Non-excitable supporting cells occupying >50% volume of neural tissue
explanation: Neural tissue structural composition regulating body sensory perception and response. Chapter 7: Structural Organisation in Animals (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

bullets: Species: Periplaneta americana
Class: Insecta (3 pairs of jointed legs)
Phylum: Arthropoda (chitinous exoskeleton)
explanation: Taxonomic hierarchy and classification position of the common nocturnal cockroach.

mnemonic: Dorsal Tergite, Ventral Strenite, Lateral Pleura
bullets: Tergites: Dorsal hardened chitinous plates
Sternites: Ventral hardened chitinous plates
Pleurites: Flexible lateral arthrodial membranes connecting plates
explanation: Hardened exoskeleton sclerite organization surrounding each body segment of cockroach.

bullets: Origin: Formed by fusion of 6 embryonic body segments
Labrum: Upper lip | Labium: Lower lip
Mandibles: Paired grinding/incising jaws
Maxillae: Paired holding appendages | Hypopharynx: Tongue-like median lobe
explanation: Triangular hypognathous head structure with biting and chewing type apparatus.

mnemonic: Tegmina Dark Opaque Mesothorax, Hindwing Membranous Transparent Metathorax
bullets: Forewings (Tegmina): Arise from mesothorax; opaque, dark, leathery, protective
Hindwings: Arise from metathorax; transparent, membranous, used in actual flight
explanation: Structural and functional distinction between the two thoracic wing pairs in cockroaches.

mnemonic: Pharynx Oesophagus Crop Gizzard Midgut Hindgut
bullets: Foregut: Pharynx -> Oesophagus -> Crop (stores food) -> Gizzard/Proventriculus (grinds food with 6 chitinous teeth)
Midgut (Mesenteron): Digestion and absorption
Hindgut: Ileum -> Colon -> Rectum
explanation: Sequential anatomical divisions of the complete digestive tract in cockroaches.

topic: Cockroach Hepatic Caeca vs Malpighian Tubules
mnemonic: Hepatic 6-8 Fore-Mid Junction, Malpighian 100-150 Mid-Hind Junction
bullets: Hepatic/Gastric Caeca: 6–8 blind tubules at Foregut-Midgut junction (secretes digestive juice)
Malpighian Tubules: 100–150 yellow thin tubules at Midgut-Hindgut junction (excretion)
explanation: Location, number, and distinct physiological functions of digestive vs excretory tubules. Chapter 7: Structural Organisation in Animals (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

bullets: Respiration: Tracheal network opening through 10 pairs of spiracles (2 thoracic, 8 abdominal)
Excretion: Uricotelic; Malpighian tubules absorb nitrogenous wastes converting to uric acid
Accessory Excretory Units: Fat body, nephrocytes, urecose glands
explanation: Respiratory spiracular system and uricotelic metabolic waste elimination pathways.

bullets: Type: Open vascular system with hemocoel cavity filled with hemolymph
Heart: 13 funnel-shaped muscular chambers along mid-dorsal line with ostia
Circulation: Pumped anteriorly into sinuses aided by 12 pairs of alary muscles
explanation: Open circulatory mechanics where blood flows freely in open tissue spaces.

bullets: Male: Testes in 4th–6th abdominal segments; Mushroom gland in 6th–7th segments
Female: 2 large ovaries in 2nd–6th segments; each ovary has 8 ovarioles (total 16)
Ootheca: Dark reddish brown capsule containing 14–16 eggs
explanation: Segmental placement of gonads and ootheca formation parameters in cockroaches.

mnemonic: 2000 Ommatidia Mosaic High Sensitivity Low Resolution
bullets: Compound Eyes: Each eye composed of ~2,000 hexagonal ommatidia
Vision Type: Mosaic vision (multiple images of an object)
Trait: High nocturnal sensitivity but lower image resolution
explanation: Visual unit composition of arthropod compound eyes specialized for night detection.

bullets: Species: Rana tigrina (Indian Bullfrog)
Poikilotherm: Cold-blooded animal (body temperature varies with environment)
Adaptations: Camouflage (mimicry), aestivation (summer sleep), hibernation (winter sleep)
explanation: Basic characteristics and survival adaptations of land-water living amphibians.

mnemonic: Smooth Smooth Skin, Fore-4 Hind-5 Digits
bullets: Skin: Smooth, moist, slippery, mucus-covered, lacks scales
Forelimbs: End in 4 digits (copulatory pad present on 1st digit in males during breeding)
Hindlimbs: Larger, muscular, end in 5 webbed digits adapted for swimming
explanation: Cutaneous characteristics and limb/digit count variations aiding locomotion. Chapter 7: Structural Organisation in Animals (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

mnemonic: Short Alimentary Canal, Bifid Tongue, Cloaca Out
bullets: Short Gut: Carnivorous nature leads to reduced intestine length
Tongue: Bilobed/bifid muscular tongue attached anteriorly to catch prey
Cloaca: Common chamber for digestive, excretory, and reproductive outlets
explanation: Anatomical digestive tract modifications suited to carnivorous diet and single excretory opening.

topic: Three Modes of Respiration in Frog
bullets: Cutaneous (Skin): Moist skin respiration in water, land, hibernation, and aestivation
Buccopharyngeal: Oral cavity lining respiration on land
Pulmonary (Lungs): Pair of elongated pink sac-like lungs used on land
explanation: Triple respiratory mechanisms enabling survival across aquatic and terrestrial habitats.

mnemonic: 3-Chambered Sinus Venosus Truncus Arteriosus Nucleated RBC
bullets: Chambers: 3-chambered heart (2 auricles + 1 ventricle)
Accessory Structures: Sinus venosus (joins right atrium), Truncus arteriosus (arises from ventricle)
Blood Cells: RBCs are oval, nucleated, and contain hemoglobin
explanation: Closed circulatory system layout with double circulation and specialized portal systems.

bullets: Hepatic Portal System: Venous connection between gut/alimentary canal and liver
Renal Portal System: Venous connection between lower body parts and kidneys
explanation: Specialized vascular bypass systems routing venous blood through intermediate organs before reaching heart.

bullets: Product: Ureotelic animal (excretes urea)
Organs: Pair of dark red compact mesonephric kidneys
Ureters: Open into cloaca; urinary bladder lies ventral to rectum opening into cloaca
explanation: Renal excretory setup filtering metabolic nitrogenous waste into urea.

bullets: Testes: Adhered to upper part of kidneys by mesorchium
Vasa Efferentia: 10–12 ductules arising from testes entering kidneys
Bidder's Canal: Kidney canal receiving vasa efferentia, carrying sperm to urogenital duct opening into cloaca
explanation: Male reproductive tract integration with kidney drainage system in frogs. Chapter 7: Structural Organisation in Animals (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

mnemonic: Hooke Cork, Leeuwenhoek Live, Brown Nucleus
bullets: Robert Hooke: Discovered cell wall / dead cork cells
Anton von Leeuwenhoek: First observed and described a living cell
Robert Brown: Discovered the cell nucleus
explanation: Historical biological milestones establishing the basic cellular structure.

mnemonic: Schleiden Botanist, Schwann Zoologist, Virchow Division
bullets: Matthias Schleiden (1838): German Botanist (all plants made of cells)
Theodore Schwann (1839): British Zoologist (animals/plants made of cells; plasma membrane)
Rudolf Virchow (1855): Omnis cellula-e-cellula (cells arise from pre-existing cells)
explanation: Key scientists who formulated and modified modern cell theory.

mnemonic: P P L O < Virus < Bacteria < RBC
bullets: Mycoplasma / PPLO: ~0.1 - 0.3 μm (smallest living cells)
Viruses: 0.02 - 0.2 μm
Typical Bacteria: 1 - 2 μm (3 - 5 μm in general)
Human RBCs: ~7.0 μm in diameter
explanation: Size ordering of prokaryotic and cellular entities required for NEET numerical comparisons.

mnemonic: G C P” (Glycocalyx, Cell wall, Plasma membrane)
bullets: Glycocalyx: Outermost layer (Capsule or Slime layer)
Cell Wall: Middle rigid layer giving shape and structural support
Plasma Membrane: Innermost selectively permeable membrane
explanation: The three-layered protective envelope present in most prokaryotic cells.

bullets: Slime Layer: Loose, gelatinous sheath preventing loss of water/nutrients
Capsule: Thick, tough, rigid outer protective layer
explanation: Two physical modifications of the outer glycocalyx layer in bacteria.

bullets: D – DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells
R – Respiration (site of respiratory enzymes)
S – Secretion processes
S – Surface area enhancement for enzymatic content
explanation: Plasma membrane invaginations in prokaryotes acting analogously to mitochondria. Chapter 8: Cell: The Unit of Life (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

mnemonic: B H F” (Basal body, Hook, Filament)
bullets: Basal Body: Embedded in cell wall and plasma membrane
Hook: Curved tubular structure connecting filament to basal body
Filament: Longest tubular portion extending outward from cell surface
explanation: Structural components of prokaryotic flagella responsible for motility.

bullets: Phosphate Granules: Store inorganic phosphate
Glycogen Granules: Reserve carbohydrate storage
Cyanophycean Granules: Nitrogenous reserve food material in BGA
explanation: Non-membrane bound reserve material structures lying free in prokaryotic cytoplasm.

bullets: Singer & Nicolson (1972): Proposed Fluid Mosaic Model
Lipids: Amphipathic phosphoglycerides arranged in bilayer
Human RBC Membrane: 52% protein, 40% lipid, 8% carbohydrate
explanation: Quasi-fluid structure enabling lateral movement of proteins within lipid bilayer.

mnemonic: Middle Lamella Pectate, Primary Elastic, Secondary Inner
bullets: Middle Lamella: Calcium/Magnesium pectate layer glueing adjacent cells
Primary Wall: Capable of growth, diminishes as cell matures
Secondary Wall: Formed on inner side (towards membrane) of mature cell
explanation: Stratified architecture of plant cell wall providing protection and structural rigidity.

bullets: G – Golgi apparatus
E – Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER & SER)
L – Lysosomes
V – Vacuoles
explanation: Group of membranous organelles whose functions are coordinated. (Mitochondria, Chloroplasts, Peroxisomes are NOT part of this system).

mnemonic: RER Ribosome Protein, SER Steroid Lipid Detox
bullets: Rough ER (RER): Bears ribosomes; active in protein synthesis and secretion
Smooth ER (SER): Lacks ribosomes; site for lipid synthesis, steroid hormones, detoxification
explanation: Structural and functional divergence between ribosome-studded and smooth ER membranes. Chapter 8: Cell: The Unit of Life (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

mnemonic: Cis Forming Convex, Trans Maturing Concave
bullets: Cis Face: Convex forming face (receives vesicles from ER)
Trans Face: Concave maturing face (releases processed vesicles)
Major Function: Glycosylation (formation of glycoproteins & glycolipids)
explanation: Structural polarity of Golgi apparatus essential for directional protein modification and routing.

bullets: Formation: Formed by packaging in Golgi apparatus
Enzymes: Rich in hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrates)
Optimal pH: Active at acidic pH (< 5.0)
explanation: Single membrane-bound digestive vesicles involved in intracellular macromolecular breakdown.

bullets: Volume: Occupies up to 90% of plant cell volume
Tonoplast: Single semi-permeable membrane enclosing vacuole
Transport: Facilitates transport of ions against concentration gradient into vacuole
explanation: Central storage organelle maintaining turgor pressure and ionic concentration in plant cells.

bullets: Outer Membrane: Continuous limiting boundary of organelle
Inner Membrane: Infolded into cristae to increase surface area for ATP synthesis
Matrix: Contains circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and enzymes for TCA cycle
explanation: Double membrane organization of powerhouse of cell producing ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.

bullets: Amyloplasts: Store carbohydrates (starch, e.g., Potato)
Aleuroplasts: Store proteins
Elaioplasts: Store oils and fats
explanation: Non-pigmented leucoplast divisions based on specific nutrient storage types.

bullets: Thylakoids: Flattened membranous sacs arranged in stacks (grana)
Stroma: Fluid containing double-stranded circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and RuBisCO
Lumen: Space enclosed by thylakoid membrane
explanation: Double membrane photosynthetic organelle containing light and dark reaction sites. Chapter 8: Cell: The Unit of Life (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

bullets: Prokaryotic / Organellar Ribosomes (70S): 50S large + 30S small subunit
Eukaryotic Cytoplasmic Ribosomes (80S): 60S large + 40S small subunit
S = Svedberg’s unit (Sedimentation coefficient measure)
explanation: Non-membrane bound protein synthesis factories discovered by George Palade (1953).

bullets: Microtubules: Tubulin protein polymers (spindle, cilia, flagella, centriole)
Intermediate Filaments: Mechanical strength (keratin, neurofilaments)
Microfilaments: Actin polymers (cell motility, cleavage furrow, cyclosis)
explanation: Network of filamentous proteinaceous structures in cytoplasm maintaining cell shape and motility.

bullets: Peripheral Doublets: 9 pairs located at periphery
Central Microtubules: 1 pair in center connected by bridge
Radial Spokes: 9 spokes connecting peripheral doublets to central sheath
explanation: Internal axonemal microtubule arrangement of eukaryotic motile appendages.

bullets: Peripheral Triplets: 9 sets of tubulin triplets located peripherally
Central Hub: Proteinaceous hub in center (lacks central microtubules = 0)
Basal Body: Centrioles form basal body of cilia and flagella
explanation: Non-membrane bound organelle containing two perpendicular centrioles organizing spindle apparatus.

bullets: Discovery: Robert Brown (1831) described nucleus
Staining: W. Flemming stained nuclear material with basic dyes and named it 'Chromatin'
explanation: Key historical landmarks in nuclear structure characterization.

bullets: Membrane: Non-membrane bound spherical structure continuous with nucleoplasm
Function: Active site for ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis
Variation: Larger and more numerous in cells actively carrying out protein synthesis
explanation: Sub-nuclear organelle responsible for ribosome subunit assembly. Chapter 8: Cell: The Unit of Life (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

mnemonic: M S A T” (Metacentric, Sub-metacentric, Acrocentric, Telocentric)
bullets: Metacentric: Centromere in middle -> 2 equal arms (V-shape)
Sub-metacentric: Slightly away from middle -> one shorter, one longer arm (L-shape)
Acrocentric: Near one end -> one extremely short, one very long arm (J-shape)
Telocentric: Terminal centromere -> single arm (I-shape)
explanation: Four morphological types of chromosomes categorized by relative centromere location.

bullets: Secondary Constriction: Non-staining, constant position constriction present on specific chromosomes
Satellite: Small fragment beyond secondary constriction
NOR: Nucleolar Organizer Region involved in nucleolus formation
explanation: Special chromosomal structural markers used in karyotype identification.

bullets: Peroxisomes: Contain catalase for H2O2 detoxification and photorespiration
Glyoxysomes: Convert lipids to carbohydrates during seed germination
Occurrence: Present in both plant and animal cells
explanation: Minute, single membrane-bound enzyme-filled vesicles present in cytoplasm.

bullets: Definition: Svedberg unit (S) measures sedimentation rate in ultracentrifuge
Indirect Measure: Reflects both density and molecular size of ribosomes
explanation: Physical unit explaining why 70S and 80S values do not sum up linearly from their subunits.

bullets: Mitochondria: Double membrane semi-autonomous organelle
Nucleus: Double nuclear envelope with perinuclear space
Chloroplast: Double membrane plastid with stroma and thylakoids
explanation: Only three cell structures possess a double-membrane envelope system.

bullets: Genome: Contain own extra-chromosomal double-stranded circular DNA
Protein Synthesis: Possess 70S ribosomes to synthesize some of their own proteins
Division: Multiply by binary fission (Endosymbiotic origin theory)
explanation: Characteristics shared by Mitochondria and Chloroplasts establishing evolutionary prokaryotic origin. Chapter 8: Cell: The Unit of Life (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

bullets: Acid-Soluble Pool (Filtrate): Molecular weight 18 to 800 Daltons (Micromolecules, biomicromolecules)
Acid-Insoluble Pool (Retentate): Molecular weight > 10,000 Daltons (Proteins, Nucleic acids, Polysaccharides)
Exception: Lipids are in retentate (< 800 Da) because of membrane vesicles.
explanation: Trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH) chemical analysis separating tissue components into two pools.

bullets: P: Phenylalanine | V: Valine | T: Threonine
T: Tryptophan | I: Isoleucine | M: Methionine
H: Histidine | A: Arginine (Semi-essential) | L: Leucine | L: Lysine
explanation: 10 essential amino acids that cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be supplied in diet.

topic: Acidic vs Basic vs Neutral Amino Acids
mnemonic: Acidic = Glu-Asp | Basic = HAL | Neutral = Val-Ala
bullets: Acidic: Glutamic acid, Aspartate (extra carboxyl group -COOH)
Basic: Histidine, Arginine, Lysine (extra amino group -NH2)
Neutral: Valine, Alanine, Glycine, Leucine
explanation: Classification based on total number of amino and carboxyl groups in the structure.

bullets: Phenylalanine: Benzene ring side chain
Tryptophan: Indole ring side chain
Tyrosine: Phenolic side chain
explanation: Amino acids possessing aromatic rings in their 'R' group structures.

topic: Amino Acid 'R' Group Variations (Glycine, Alanine, Serine)
bullets: Glycine: R = -H (simplest, optically inactive/achiral)
Alanine: R = -CH3 (methyl group)
Serine: R = -CH2OH (hydroxy-methyl group)
explanation: Structural variations of the variable 'R' side chain on the alpha carbon of amino acids.

bullets: Zwitterion: Dipolar ion with both positive (-NH3+) and negative (-COO-) charges
Net Charge: Zero net charge at specific pH (isoelectric point)
Behavior: Acts as amphoteric species in solution
explanation: Structural state of amino acids in aqueous solutions across varying pH levels. Chapter 9: Biomolecules (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

topic: Fatty Acids: Palmitic vs Arachidonic Acid
bullets: Palmitic Acid: Saturated fatty acid with 16 carbons (including carboxyl carbon)
Arachidonic Acid: Unsaturated fatty acid with 20 carbons (including carboxyl carbon)
explanation: Carbon counts of key saturated and unsaturated fatty acids highlighted in NCERT.

bullets: Glycerol: Simple lipid identified chemically as 1,2,3-trihydroxypropane
Triglyceride: 1 Glycerol esterified with 3 Fatty Acid molecules via ester bonds
explanation: Chemical structure of neutral fats formed by esterification reactions.

bullets: Composition: Fatty acids esterified to glycerol with a phosphate group attached to choline
Location: Major constituent of cell membranes
explanation: Conjugated, phosphorus-containing lipid critical for cellular membrane architecture.

mnemonic: PURE As Gold, CUT the Py
bullets: Purines (Double ring): Adenine (A), Guanine (G)
Pyrimidines (Single ring): Cytosine (C), Uracil (U), Thymine (T)
explanation: Nitrogenous base ring structures constituting nucleic acid monomers.

mnemonic: Nucleoside = Base + Sugar | Nucleotide = Base + Sugar + Phosphate
bullets: Nucleoside: Nitrogenous base + Pentose sugar (e.g., Adenosine, Uridine)
Nucleotide: Nucleoside + Phosphate group via phosphoester bond (e.g., Adénylic acid)
explanation: Fundamental monomeric distinction in nucleic acid biochemistry.

mnemonic: A T A E D P R
bullets: Alkaloids: Morphine, Codeine | Toxins: Abrin, Ricin
Lectins: Concanavalin A | Drugs: Vinblastine, Curcumin
Polymeric Substances: Rubber, Gums, Cellulose | Essential Oils: Lemon grass oil
explanation: NCERT Table 9.3 list of non-primary plant/fungal biochemical products. Chapter 9: Biomolecules (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

mnemonic: Primary Direct Function, Secondary Ecological Role
bullets: Primary Metabolites: Known physiological functions; involved directly in growth (e.g., sugars, amino acids)
Secondary Metabolites: No direct role in primary development; ecological importance (e.g., alkaloids, flavonoids)
explanation: Functional division between essential operational biomolecules and specialized natural products.

bullets: Reducing Sugars: Free aldehyde/ketone group available (All monosaccharides, Maltose, Lactose)
Non-Reducing Sugars: Anomeric carbons locked in glycosidic bond (Sucrose, Starch, Cellulose)
explanation: Ability of carbohydrate functional groups to reduce Fehling's/Benedict's reagents.

bullets: Right End: Reducing end of polysaccharide chain
Left End: Non-reducing end of polysaccharide chain
explanation: Directional chemical polarity present in complex carbohydrate polymers like glycogen.

topic: Starch vs Cellulose vs Glycogen Structures
mnemonic: Starch Helical Iodine Blue, Cellulose Straight Unbranched
bullets: Starch: Helical secondary structure; traps I2 molecules giving blue color
Cellulose: Linear unbranched beta-1,4 polymer; cannot hold I2 (no blue color)
Glycogen: Highly branched alpha-1,4 and 1,6 storage polymer in animals
explanation: Structural variations explaining iodine test behavior among plant and animal glucans.

bullets: Monomer: N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) - a modified complex homopolysaccharide
Occurrence: Fungal cell wall and Arthropod chitinous exoskeleton
explanation: Nitrogen-containing structural polysaccharide widely distributed in fungi and invertebrates.

mnemonic: P S T Q” (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Quaternary)
bullets: Primary: Sequence of amino acids held by peptide bonds (N-terminal left, C-terminal right)
Secondary: Local folding into alpha-helix (right-handed) or beta-pleated sheet
Tertiary: 3D folding giving functional biological conformation (e.g., myoglobin)
Quaternary: Assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits (e.g., Adult Hemoglobin = 2a + 2b)
explanation: Four hierarchical tiers of structural complexity in functional protein molecules. Chapter 9: Biomolecules (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

bullets: Proteins: Peptide bond (between -COOH and -NH2)
Carbohydrates: Glycosidic bond (between monosaccharides)
Nucleic Acids: Phosphodiester bond (between 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate)
Lipids: Ester bond (between glycerol -OH and fatty acid -COOH)
explanation: Diagnostic chemical linkages holding together distinct classes of biological polymers.

bullets: Helical Pitch: 34 Å (3.4 nm) per full turn
Base Pairs per Turn: 10 bp per complete 360-degree turn
Rise per Base Pair: 3.4 Å (0.34 nm) distance between adjacent base steps
explanation: Watson-Crick double-helical structural metrics for classical B-form DNA.

bullets: Collagen: Most abundant protein in the animal world
RuBisCO: Most abundant protein in the entire biosphere
explanation: Biological abundance rankings frequently queried in NEET direct questions.

mnemonic: O T H L I L
bullets: Class 1: Oxidoreductases / Dehydrogenases | Class 2: Transferases
Class 3: Hydrolases | Class 4: Lyases (cleave without water)
Class 5: Isomerases | Class 6: Ligases (join molecules using ATP)
explanation: Six major functional classes of enzymes established by the International Union of Biochemistry.

bullets: Transition State: Unstable high-energy intermediate state during substrate conversion
Mechanism: Enzymes lower activation energy requirement without changing equilibrium point
explanation: Thermodynamic mechanism by which biocatalysts accelerate metabolic reaction rates.

bullets: Mechanism: Inhibitor closely resembles substrate in structure (competes for active site)
Kinetic Effect: Km increases (substrate affinity appears lower); Vmax remains unchanged
Classic Example: Malonate inhibits Succinic Dehydrogenase
explanation: Diagnostic kinetic changes and classic biochemical example of competitive inhibition. Chapter 9: Biomolecules (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

bullets: Holoenzyme: Complete, catalytically active enzyme complex
Apoenzyme: Protein portion of the enzyme (inactive alone)
Cofactor: Non-protein moiety required for enzyme activity
explanation: Structural breakdown of functional biocatalytic complexes.

mnemonic: P C M” (Prosthetic, Coenzyme, Metal Ion)
bullets: Prosthetic Groups: Tightly bound organic compounds (e.g., Haem in peroxidase/catalase)
Coenzymes: Transiently bound organic compounds, often vitamins (e.g., NAD, NADP contain Niacin)
Metal Ions: Coordination bonds with active site and substrate (e.g., Zn2+ for Carboxypeptidase)
explanation: Three distinct categories of non-protein cofactors and their binding characteristics.

mnemonic: T P S” (Temperature, pH, Substrate Concentration)
bullets: Temperature & pH: Show bell-shaped optimum curve; extremes cause denaturation
Substrate Conc: Increases rate until Vmax is reached (saturation of active sites)
explanation: Physical parameters modulating biocatalytic reaction rates.

bullets: Carbonic Anhydrase: Speeds up CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3 reaction by 10 million times
Rate: Produces 600,000 molecules of H2CO3 per second (vs 200/hr without enzyme)
explanation: Extreme catalytic speed comparison cited in NCERT for carbonic anhydrase.

mnemonic: Anabolic Builds (Consumes ATP), Catabolic Breaks (Yields ATP)
bullets: Anabolic: Synthesis pathways, endergonic (e.g., Acetic acid -> Cholesterol)
Catabolic: Degradative pathways, exergonic (e.g., Glucose -> Lactic acid via glycolysis)
explanation: Energy coupling and structural outcome differences between metabolic pathways.

bullets: Concept: The living state is a non-equilibrium steady state capable of doing work
System Rule: Systems at equilibrium cannot perform work; metabolism prevents reaching equilibrium
explanation: Fundamental thermodynamic definition of cellular life and metabolic flux. Chapter 9: Biomolecules (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

bullets: I: Interphase (> 95% of cell cycle duration)
M: M-Phase / Mitotic Phase (< 5% duration)
Phases: G1 → S → G2 → M Phase (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase)
explanation: The sequential progression of events dividing cell cycle into resting/prep phase and active division phase.

topic: Duration of Human vs Yeast Cell Cycle
bullets: Human Cells in Culture: Divide once in approx. 24 hours
Yeast (Saccharomyces): Completes cell cycle in approx. 90 minutes
explanation: Specific duration benchmarks emphasized in NCERT for eukaryote cell division rates.

bullets: G1 Phase (Gap 1): First growth phase, active transcription/translation, organelle duplication
S Phase (Synthesis): DNA replication in nucleus, centriole duplication in cytoplasm
G2 Phase (Gap 2): Protein synthesis (tubulin), preparation for mitosis
explanation: Sub-phases of Interphase preceding nuclear division.

topic: DNA Amount vs Chromosome Number in S Phase
bullets: DNA Content: Doubles from 2C to 4C during S phase
Chromosome Number: Remains unchanged at 2N (diploid)
explanation: Crucial numerical concept: S phase replicates DNA content without increasing the total chromosome count.

bullets: DNA Replication: Occurs inside the Nucleus during S phase
Centriole Duplication: Occurs in the Cytoplasm during S phase in animal cells
explanation: Spatial localization of duplication events during S phase.

bullets: G0 State: Cells exit G1 phase to enter an inactive stage
Characteristics: Metabolically active, no longer proliferate unless requested (e.g., heart cells, neurons)
explanation: Non-dividing resting state entered by specialized mature cells. Chapter 10: Cell Cycle and Cell Division (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

bullets: P: Prophase (Chromatin condensation starts)
M: Metaphase (Equatorial alignment)
A: Anaphase (Sister chromatids separate)
T: Telophase (Nuclear membrane reappears)
explanation: The sequential order of nuclear division (karyokinesis) steps in mitosis.

bullets: Chromatin: Condenses into compact mitotic chromosomes
Centrosomes: Move to opposite poles and radiate asters (spindle fibers)
Organelles: Nucleolus, Golgi, ER, and nuclear envelope disappear by late prophase
explanation: Key morphological transformations occurring in the first stage of karyokinesis.

bullets: Alignment: Chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate (equatorial plate)
Attachment: Kinetochores attach to spindle fibers from opposite poles
Study: Best stage to study chromosome morphology/structure under microscope
explanation: Maximum condensation of chromosomes occurs at metaphase, making shape analysis optimal.

bullets: Centromere Split: Centromeres divide, splitting sister chromatids into daughter chromosomes
Migration: Daughter chromosomes move to opposite poles led by centromeres (arms trail behind)
explanation: Shortest stage of mitosis where genetic material is physically separated.

bullets: Decondensation: Chromosomes cluster at poles and lose identity
Reformation: Nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi complex, and ER reform
explanation: The final phase of karyokinesis where two distinct daughter nuclei are reconstructed.

mnemonic: Animal Furrow Centripetal, Plant Cell-Plate Centrifugal
bullets: Animal Cells: Plasma membrane cleavage furrow deepens centripetally (outside to inside)
Plant Cells: Rigid wall requires cell-plate (phragmoplast precursor) growing centrifugally (center to outside)
explanation: Cytoplasmic division mechanism divergence due to plant cell wall constraints. Chapter 10: Cell Cycle and Cell Division (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

bullets: Definition: Liquid endosperm of coconut is a classic example of multinucleate condition
Cause: Repeated nuclear divisions (karyokinesis) not followed by cell division (cytokinesis)
explanation: Formation of multinucleated cells due to incomplete cell division cycles.

mnemonic: G R R E” (Growth, Repair, Replacement, Equational)
bullets: G: Growth of multicellular organisms
R: Repair and cell replacement (epidermis, lining of gut, blood cells)
E: Equational division preserving genetic identity (2n → 2n)
explanation: Biological purpose of mitotic division in somatic tissues.

mnemonic: Meiosis I Reductional, Meiosis II Equational
bullets: Meiosis I: Heterotypic / Reductional division (2n → 1n), homologous pairs separate
Meiosis II: Homotypic / Equational division (1n → 1n), sister chromatids separate
explanation: Fundamental distinction between the two consecutive divisions of meiosis.

bullets: L: Leptotene | Z: Zygotene | P: Pachytene
D: Diplotene | D: Diakinesis
explanation: Chronological order of the 5 detailed stages of Prophase I in Meiosis I.

bullets: Visual: Chromosomes become gradually visible under light microscope
Process: Compaction of chromosomes continues throughout Leptotene
explanation: Initial stage where chromatin fibers condense into visible thin threads.

bullets: Synapsis: Pairing of homologous chromosomes
Structure: Formation of Synaptonemal Complex
Result: Bivalent or Tetrad complex becomes visible
explanation: Homologous chromosome pairing mediated by proteinaceous synaptonemal structures. Chapter 10: Cell Cycle and Cell Division (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

bullets: Crossing Over: Exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids
Enzyme: Mediated by Recombinase enzyme complex
Structure: Recombination nodules clearly visible on bivalents
explanation: The key stage responsible for genetic variation through non-sister chromatid exchange.

bullets: Dissolution: Synaptonemal complex dissolves
Separation: Homologues separate except at sites of crossovers
Chiasmata: X-shaped structures visible (can last months/years in oocytes of vertebrates)
explanation: Unpairing stage revealing X-shaped crossover points called chiasmata.

bullets: Terminalization: Chiasmata shift towards ends of chromosomes
Transition: Nucleolus disappears, nuclear envelope breaks down
Mark: Represents transition to Metaphase I
explanation: Final stage of Prophase I preparing chromosomes for spindle alignment.

mnemonic: Metaphase I = Double Plate (Bivalents) | Metaphase II = Single Plate
bullets: Metaphase I: Bivalent homologous pairs align on double equatorial plate
Metaphase II: Individual chromosomes align on single equatorial plate (like Mitosis)
explanation: Key structural difference in equatorial alignment between Meiosis I and II.

mnemonic: Anaphase I = Homologues Separate (No Centromere Split) | Anaphase II = Centromeres Split
bullets: Anaphase I: Homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles; centromeres DO NOT divide
Anaphase II: Sister chromatids separate due to centromere splitting
explanation: Critical mechanical distinction explaining why Meiosis I reduces ploidy while Meiosis II preserves it.

mnemonic: Interkinesis = Short Pause, NO DNA Replication
bullets: Definition: Stage between Meiosis I and Meiosis II
Feature: Generally short-lived; NO replication of DNA takes place during interkinesis
explanation: Intervening period between meiotic divisions without S-phase replication. Chapter 10: Cell Cycle and Cell Division (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

bullets: Chromosome Number: Specific chromosome number conserved across generations in sexually reproducing species
Genetic Variability: Increases variations in populations from generation to generation
explanation: Evolutionary importance of meiotic division in sexually reproducing organisms.

bullets: G1/S Checkpoint: Main decision point (restriction point) for cell division commitment
G2/M Checkpoint: Checks DNA replication completeness and damage
Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC): Ensures all kinetochores are attached to spindle fibers in metaphase
explanation: Quality control mechanisms ensuring accurate transmission of genetic material.

mnemonic: Cyclin B + CDK1 = MPF (Maturation Promoting Factor)
bullets: CDKs (Cyclin Dependent Kinases): Catalytic subunits requiring binding to cyclins for activity
MPF: Complex of Cyclin B and CDK1 driving transition from G2 phase into M phase
explanation: Biochemical engine controlling phase transitions in eukaryotic cell cycles.

bullets: Mechanism: Inhibits microtubule polymerization by binding tubulin protein
Effect: Prevents spindle fiber formation, arresting cells at Metaphase
Application: Induces polyploidy in plant breeding
explanation: Chemical agent commonly tested in NEET for metaphase arrest and chromosome doubling.

bullets: Process: Direct nuclear constriction without spindle formation or chromosome condensation
Occurrence: Prokaryotes (binary fission), unicellular eukaryotes (e.g., Amoeba), and fetal membranes
explanation: Primitive or specialized division method lacking structured mitotic apparatus.

bullets: 1 Bivalent: Pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes
Chromatid Count: Consists of 4 chromatids (hence called a Tetrad)
Centromere Count: 2 centromeres present per bivalent
explanation: Quantitative conversion relationships frequently tested in numerical NEET questions. Chapter 10: Cell Cycle and Cell Division (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

mnemonic: Priestly Oxygen, Ingenhousz Light, Engelmann Spectrum
bullets: Joseph Priestley: Discovered O2 in 1774 using bell jar and mint plant
Jan Ingenhousz: Showed sunlight is essential for O2 release in aquatic plants
T.W. Engelmann: Discovered first action spectrum using Cladophora and aerobic bacteria
explanation: Historical contributions identifying essential components and action spectrum of photosynthesis.

mnemonic: Water Gives Oxygen, H2S Gives Sulfur
bullets: Cornelius van Niel: Demonstrated photosynthesis is a light-dependent redox process
Purple and Green Sulfur Bacteria: Use H2S instead of H2O, yielding sulfur oxidation product
Conclusion: O2 released in green plants comes from H2O, not CO2
explanation: Microbiological studies proving water as the source of oxygen in plant photosynthesis.

mnemonic: A-Blue Green, B-Yellow Green, X-Yellow, C-Yellow Orange
bullets: Chlorophyll a: Bright or blue green in chromatogram
Chlorophyll b: Yellow green
Xanthophylls: Yellow
Carotenoids: Yellow to yellow-orange
explanation: Paper chromatography separation colors of photosynthetic leaf pigments.

bullets: Chlorophyll a: Essential primary pigment present in all oxygenic photosynthetic organisms
Action Spectrum: Peaks match absorption spectrum of Chlorophyll a (Blue & Red regions)
explanation: Chlorophyll a functions as the main reaction center pigment responsible for light energy conversion.

bullets: Broaden Spectrum: Absorb wider range of light wavelengths and transfer energy to Chl-a
Protect: Protect Chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation (photobleaching)
explanation: Role of Chlorophyll b, Xanthophylls, and Carotenoids as LHC antenna molecules.

bullets: LHC (Antennae): Hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins harvesting photons
Reaction Center: Single Chlorophyll a molecule that initiates electron transfer
explanation: Structural organization of Photosystems I and II embedded in thylakoid membranes. Chapter 11: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

mnemonic: PS Two Six-Eighty, PS One Seven-Hundred
bullets: PS II: Reaction center Chlorophyll a absorbs at 680 nm (P680)
PS I: Reaction center Chlorophyll a absorbs at 700 nm (P700)
explanation: Peak absorption wavelengths distinguishing Photosystem II and Photosystem I reaction centers.

mnemonic: PS II → Pheo → PQ → Cyt b6f → PC → PS I → Fd → NADP+
bullets: PS II to ETC: P680 → Pheophytin → Plastoquinone (PQ) → Cytochrome b6f → Plastocyanin (PC)
PS I to NADP+: P700 → Ferredoxin (Fd) → NADP+ Reductase → NADPH
explanation: Non-cyclic electron transport path across thylakoid membrane driven by redox potential gradient.

bullets: Location: Oxygen Evolving Complex (OEC) associated with PS II on the lumen side of thylakoid
Reaction: 2 H2O → 4 H+ + O2 + 4 e-
Essential Minerals: Mn2+ (Manganese), Cl- (Chlorine), Ca2+ (Calcium)
explanation: Photolytic cleavage of water providing electrons to replace those lost by P680.

mnemonic: Non-Cyclic Yields ATP, NADPH, and Oxygen
bullets: ATP: Produced via proton gradient across thylakoid membrane
NADPH: Reduced coenzyme formed on stroma side
O2: Released into lumen and diffuses out as byproduct
explanation: Output generated when both PS II and PS I operate in series during non-cyclic electron transport.

mnemonic: Stroma Lamellae PS I ATP Only
bullets: Location: Stroma lamellae membranes (lacks PS II and NADP reductase enzyme)
Conditions: Light wavelength beyond 680 nm or low CO2 availability
Product: Produces ATP ONLY (No NADPH, No O2)
explanation: Cyclic electron flow around PS I supplying additional ATP required for dark reaction assimilation.

bullets: Photolysis: H+ released in lumen by water splitting
PQ Pump: H+ pumped from stroma into lumen by PQ hydrogen carrier
NADP Reduction: H+ consumed in stroma by NADP+ reductase
explanation: Causes of high proton concentration in lumen and low in stroma forming a pH gradient. Chapter 11: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

mnemonic: CF0 Embedded Membrane, CF1 Protrudes Stroma
bullets: CF0: Transmembrane channel facilitating proton diffusion across membrane
CF1: Headpiece protruding into stroma, undergoes conformational change to form ATP
explanation: Structural arrangement of coupling factor ATP synthase driving photophosphorylation.

topic: Primary Acceptor in C3 vs C4 Cycle
mnemonic: C3 Accepts RuBP, C4 Accepts PEP
bullets: C3 Cycle: RuBP (5-Carbon keto sugar) is primary CO2 acceptor
C4 Cycle: PEP (3-Carbon Phosphoenolpyruvate) is primary CO2 acceptor in mesophyll
explanation: Primary CO2 accepting molecules initiating C3 and C4 photosynthetic pathways.

topic: First Stable Product in C3 vs C4 Cycle
bullets: C3 Pathway: 3-PGA (3-Phosphoglyceric acid - 3 Carbon acid)
C4 Pathway: OAA (Oxaloacetic acid - 4 Carbon dicarboxylic acid)
explanation: First stable radio-labeled CO2 fixation products giving C3 and C4 cycles their names.

bullets: Carboxylation: CO2 combines with RuBP catalyzed by RuBisCO to form 3-PGA
Reduction: Phosphorylation and reduction of 3-PGA to form Triose Phosphate (G3P)
Regeneration: RuBP acceptor regenerated for cycle continuation
explanation: Three sequential steps required to fix carbon dioxide in all photosynthetic plants.

topic: ATP and NADPH Requirement per CO2 Fixed in C3
bullets: Per CO2 Fixed: 2 ATP + 2 NADPH in Reduction, 1 ATP in Regeneration = 3 ATP, 2 NADPH
For 1 Glucose (6 CO2): 18 ATP and 12 NADPH consumed
explanation: Energetic cost required during Calvin cycle for fixing one molecule of carbon dioxide vs one hexose.

bullets: High CO2 / Low O2: Acts as Carboxylase driving C3 photosynthetic carbon fixation
High O2 / Low CO2: Acts as Oxygenase initiating wasteful Photorespiration
explanation: Bifunctional enzymatic activity of Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase depending on gas ratio. Chapter 11: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

topic: Kranz Anatomy Features in C4 Plants
mnemonic: Kranz = Wreath Bundle Sheath Thick Walls
bullets: Wreath Alignment: Bundle sheath cells arranged in concentric layers around vascular bundles
Characteristics: Large chloroplasts, agranal, thick impervious cell walls, no intercellular spaces
explanation: Specialized leaf internal anatomy characteristic of tropical C4 grasses (e.g., Maize, Sugarcane, Sorghum).

topic: Location of Enzymes in C4 Plants
bullets: Mesophyll Cells: Contain PEP carboxylase (lacks RuBisCO); initial C4 acid fixation
Bundle Sheath Cells: Contain RuBisCO (lacks PEPCase); C3 Calvin cycle site
explanation: Spatial separation of enzymes in C4 plants concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO.

bullets: Mesophyll: PEP + CO2 → OAA (4C) → Malic/Aspartic acid (4C)
Transport: C4 acid transported to Bundle Sheath
Bundle Sheath: C4 acid decarboxylated to C3 acid + CO2; CO2 enters Calvin cycle
Return: C3 acid transported back to mesophyll to regenerate PEP
explanation: Hatch and Slack pathway pump mechanism transferring fixed carbon between cell types.

topic: ATP and NADPH Cost for 1 Glucose in C4
bullets: C3 Standard Cost: 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose
C4 Additional Cost: 12 extra ATP for PEP regeneration (total 30 ATP + 12 NADPH)
explanation: Higher energy requirement in C4 plants compensated by elimination of photorespiratory loss.

bullets: C: Chloroplast (RuBP + O2 → 3-PGA + 2-Phosphoglycolate)
P: Peroxisome (Glycolate → Glyoxylate → Glycine)
M: Mitochondria (Glycine → Serine + CO2 released)
explanation: Three cellular organelles involved in the rescue photorespiratory pathway.

mnemonic: No Sugar, No ATP, Consumes O2, Releases CO2
bullets: Wasteful Process: Neither synthesizes sugar nor ATP/NADPH
Carbon Loss: Loses up to 25% of fixed carbon as CO2 in mitochondria
explanation: Why photorespiration reduces photosynthetic efficiency and crop yield in C3 plants. Chapter 11: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

mnemonic: Open Night Acid, Close Day Calv
bullets: Night: Stomata open; CO2 fixed by PEPCase into Organic Acids (Malic acid stored in vacuole)
Day: Stomata closed; Malic acid decarboxylated to release CO2 for Calvin cycle
explanation: Temporal separation of carbon fixation adapting succulent xerophytes (e.g., Pineapple, Opuntia) to water stress.

bullets: Law Statement: If a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value
Core Factor: The limiting factor directly affects process rate if its quantity is changed
explanation: Ecophysiological principle governing photosynthetic reaction rates under multiple variable conditions.

bullets: Saturation Level: Light saturation occurs at 10% of full sunlight
Limiting Condition: Light is rarely a limiting factor in nature except for shade/canopy plants
explanation: Irradiance threshold beyond which further increases in light intensity do not increase photosynthetic rate.

topic: CO2 Saturation Levels in C3 vs C4 Plants
bullets: C4 Plants: Saturation reached at low CO2 concentration (~360 μL/L)
C3 Plants: Saturation reached only at higher CO2 concentration (~450 μL/L)
explanation: Differential carbon dioxide response curves utilized in greenhouse fertilization (e.g., tomatoes, bell peppers).

topic: Temperature Optimum for C3 vs C4 Plants
bullets: C3 Plants: Optimum lower (20–25°C) due to increased photorespiration at higher temperatures
C4 Plants: Optimum higher (30–40°C) as C4 mechanism prevents photorespiration
explanation: Thermal adaptation differences between temperate C3 species and tropical C4 species.

topic: Water Stress Indirect Effect on Photosynthesis
mnemonic: Water Stress Closes Stomata, Wilts Leaves
bullets: Stomatal Closure: Reduces CO2 availability to mesophyll cells
Leaf Wilting: Reduces surface area of leaves and metabolic activity
explanation: Indirect physiological mechanisms by which water deficit limits rate of photosynthesis. Chapter 11: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

mnemonic: Carbs First, Fats Next, Proteins Last
bullets: Primary Substrate: Carbohydrates (Glucose) are oxidized first
Floating Respiration: When fats or carbohydrates are used as respiratory substrate
Protoplasmic Respiration: When cellular proteins are oxidized under starvation
explanation: Order of respiratory substrate utilization in cellular metabolism under varying metabolic states.

mnemonic: E M P = Embden, Meyerhof, Parnas
bullets: E: Gustav Embden
M: Otto Meyerhof
P: J. Parnas
explanation: Three scientists who elucidated the complete 10-step metabolic pathway of glycolysis.

bullets: Location: Occurs in Cytoplasm (Cytosol) of all living cells
Oxygen Dependence: Does NOT require molecular O2; common step to both aerobic & anaerobic respiration
explanation: Core cellular location and universal evolutionary feature of the glycolytic pathway.

bullets: G: Glucose → G: Glucose-6-Phosphate (Hexokinase)
F: Fructose-6-Phosphate → F: Fructose-1,6-Bisphosphate (PFK)
G: Glyceraldehyde-3-Phosphate (G3P / PGAL) + DHAP
explanation: Preparatory/cleavage phase of glycolysis requiring consumption of 2 ATP molecules.

bullets: 1,3-BPG: 1,3-Bisphosphoglyceric acid (generates NADH)
3-PGA: 3-Phosphoglyceric acid (generates ATP)
2-PGA: 2-Phosphoglyceric acid
PEP: Phosphoenolpyruvate (Enolase releases H2O)
Pyruvate: Pyruvic acid (generates ATP)
explanation: Payoff phase of glycolysis where energy is harvested as ATP and reduced coenzyme NADH.

bullets: Enzyme: Phosphofructokinase (PFK) converts Fructose-6-P to Fructose-1,6-BP
Significance: Rate-limiting pacemaker enzyme irreversible step
explanation: Primary control point regulating metabolic flux through the glycolytic pathway. Chapter 12: Respiration in Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

bullets: Gross Output: 4 ATP synthesized via substrate-level phosphorylation
Net Output: 2 ATP (4 made - 2 spent in prep phase)
Reducing Power: 2 NADH + 2 H+
End Product: 2 molecules of Pyruvic acid (3-Carbon)
explanation: Net stoichiometry output per molecule of glucose processed in glycolysis.

bullets: Step 7: 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate → 3-Phosphoglycerate (Phosphoglycerate Kinase)
Step 10: Phosphoenolpyruvate → Pyruvate (Pyruvate Kinase)
explanation: Direct synthesis of ATP without participation of the electron transport chain.

bullets: Enzymes: Pyruvate Decarboxylase + Alcohol Dehydrogenase
Products: Ethanol (C2H5OH) + CO2 + 2 ATP
Organism: Occurs in Yeast under anaerobic conditions
explanation: Anaerobic breakdown of pyruvate producing ethanol and releasing carbon dioxide gas.

bullets: Threshold: Yeast poison themselves to death when alcohol concentration reaches ~13%
Implication: Natural fermented beverages (wine, beer) cannot exceed 13% alcohol without distillation
explanation: Toxicity limit of ethanol concentration in naturally fermented yeast cultures.

bullets: Enzyme: Lactate Dehydrogenase (requires Zn2+)
Products: Lactic acid (3-Carbon) with ZERO CO2 released
Site: Occurs in human muscle cells during strenuous exercise & LAB bacteria
explanation: Anaerobic reduction of pyruvate directly to lactic acid without decarboxylation.

mnemonic: Less Than Seven Percent Energy Released
bullets: Energy Yield: < 7% of total energy in glucose is released during fermentation
Safety Hazard: Both alcoholic and lactic fermentation are hazardous and yield very little ATP
explanation: Low thermodynamic efficiency of anaerobic glucose catabolism. Chapter 12: Respiration in Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 2

bullets: Location: Mitochondrial Matrix
Enzyme: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase complex (requires Mg2+, TPP, NAD+, CoA)
Reaction: Pyruvate (3C) + CoA + NAD+ → Acetyl-CoA (2C) + CO2 + NADH
explanation: Oxidative decarboxylation connecting cytosol glycolytic product with mitochondrial Kreb's cycle.

bullets: Scientist: Hans Krebs (Nobel laureate)
Synonyms: TCA Cycle (Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle) / Citric Acid Cycle
Location: Matrix of Mitochondria
explanation: Central cyclic metabolic pathway for complete oxidation of acetyl units in aerobic organisms.

mnemonic: Can I Keep Selling Sex For Money Officer?
bullets: C: Citrate (6C) | I: Isocitrate (6C)
K: alpha-Ketoglutarate (5C) | S: Succinyl-CoA (4C)
S: Succinate (4C) | F: Fumarate (4C)
M: Malate (4C) | O: Oxaloacetate / OAA (4C)
explanation: Mnemonic sequence of organic acid intermediates formed in one turn of the TCA cycle.

mnemonic: Citrate to alpha-KG, alpha-KG to Succinyl-CoA
bullets: Step 1 (6C → 5C): Isocitrate → alpha-Ketoglutarate + CO2
Step 2 (5C → 4C): alpha-Ketoglutarate → Succinyl-CoA + CO2
explanation: Two decarboxylation events releasing 2 molecules of CO2 per acetyl unit in TCA cycle.

topic: Substrate Level Phosphorylation in Kreb's Cycle
bullets: Step: Conversion of Succinyl-CoA (4C) to Succinic acid (4C)
Product: Synthesizes 1 GTP directly, which transfers phosphate to form 1 ATP
explanation: The single direct high-energy phosphate bond generation step in the TCA cycle.

topic: FADH2 Generation Site in Kreb's Cycle
bullets: Step: Oxidation of Succinate (4C) to Fumarate (4C)
Enzyme: Succinate Dehydrogenase (bound to inner mitochondrial membrane / Complex II)
Output: 1 FADH2 generated
explanation: Specific enzymatic step producing reduced flavin adenine dinucleotide. Chapter 12: Respiration in Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 3

topic: Total Yield per Turn of Kreb's Cycle
bullets: Per Acetyl-CoA (1 Turn): 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 ATP + 2 CO2
Per Glucose (2 Turns): 6 NADH + 2 FADH2 + 2 ATP + 4 CO2
explanation: Stoichiometric products from complete TCA cycle processing per acetyl group vs per original glucose.

bullets: Location: Embedded in Inner Mitochondrial Membrane (Cristae)
Purpose: Transfer electrons from NADH/FADH2 to oxygen while pumping protons to intermembrane space
explanation: Structural site of respiratory chain complexes driving oxidative phosphorylation.

bullets: Complex I: NADH Dehydrogenase
Complex II: Succinate Dehydrogenase (FADH2)
Complex III: Cytochrome bc1 complex
Complex IV: Cytochrome c Oxidase (contains Cyt a, a3, 2 Cu centers)
Complex V: ATP Synthase
explanation: Five protein complexes that constitute the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

mnemonic: Ubiquinone Inside Membrane, Cyt-c Outside Inner Membrane
bullets: Ubiquinone (UQ/CoQ): Lipid-soluble mobile carrier within inner membrane; receives e- from C1 and C2
Cytochrome c: Small mobile protein attached to outer surface of inner membrane; transfers e- between C3 and C4
explanation: Diffusible electron shuttles facilitating transfer between membrane-bound complexes.

topic: ATP Yield per NADH vs FADH2
bullets: 1 NADH: Pumps more H+ (enters at Complex I) → Yields ~3 ATP (2.5 modern)
1 FADH2: Bypasses Complex I (enters at Complex II) → Yields ~2 ATP (1.5 modern)
explanation: Phosphorylation potential and ATP equivalency of reduced electron donors in NCERT.

mnemonic: Oxygen Terminal Electron Acceptor Forms Water
bullets: Role: Oxygen acts as ultimate hydrogen and electron acceptor at Complex IV
Reaction: 1/2 O2 + 2 H+ + 2 e- → H2O (Metabolic water)
explanation: Essential role of molecular oxygen removing spent electrons to keep ETS functioning. Chapter 12: Respiration in Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 4

mnemonic: Protons Flow Intermembrane to Matrix via F0
bullets: F0 Head/Channel: Integral membrane channel through which 2 H+ pass
F1 Headpiece: Peripheral matrix portion synthesizing ATP from ADP + Pi
Direction: Protons cross back from Intermembrane space into Matrix
explanation: Chemiosmotic mechanism of ATP generation powered by proton motive force in mitochondria.

bullets: Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH (6 ATP) = 8 ATP
Link Reaction: 2 NADH (6 ATP) = 6 ATP
Kreb's Cycle: 2 ATP + 6 NADH (18 ATP) + 2 FADH2 (4 ATP) = 24 ATP
Total Net Output: 38 ATP per glucose molecule (NCERT standard calculation)
explanation: Theoretical maximum ATP yield generated during complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule.

bullets: Catabolism: Breakdown of substrates to release energy
Anabolism: Intermediates withdrawn for synthesis (e.g., Acetyl-CoA for fatty acids, OAA/alpha-KG for amino acids)
explanation: Why respiratory pathway is correctly termed amphibolic rather than purely catabolic.

mnemonic: RQ = Volume CO2 Evolved / Volume O2 Consumed
bullets: Definition: Ratio of volume of CO2 evolved to volume of O2 consumed in respiration
Dependency: Depends strictly upon the chemical nature of respiratory substrate being used
explanation: Diagnostic numerical index used to identify the respiratory substrate oxidized by tissue.

topic: RQ Values of Carbohydrates, Fats, Proteins
mnemonic: Carb One, Fat Point Seven, Protein Point Nine
bullets: Carbohydrates (Glucose): RQ = 1.0 (Equal CO2 evolved and O2 consumed)
Fats (Tripalmitin): RQ = 0.7 (More O2 required for oxidation)
Proteins: RQ = 0.9
explanation: Specific numerical RQ values for major organic nutrient categories.

topic: RQ of Organic Acids & Anaerobic Respiration
mnemonic: Organic Acids More Than 1, Anaerobic Infinite
bullets: Organic Acids (Malic/Oxalic Acid): RQ > 1 (e.g., Malic acid RQ = 1.33)
Anaerobic Respiration: RQ = Infinity (CO2 evolved without O2 consumption: x / 0)
Succulents at Night: RQ = 0 (CO2 absorbed without release to form acids)
explanation: Extreme RQ values observed under specialized metabolic conditions and substrates. Chapter 12: Respiration in Plants (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 5

bullets: Indeterminate: Unlimited capacity to grow throughout life due to meristems
Open Form: New cells are continually being added to the plant body
Measurable: Measured by dry weight, fresh weight, cell number, area, or volume
Irreversible: Permanent increase in size of an organ/cell driven by protoplasm increase
explanation: Fundamental attributes defining plant growth at cellular and organ levels.

bullets: Meristematic Phase: Dense protoplasm, large nuclei, abundant plasmodesmata
Elongation Phase: Increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, new cell wall deposition
Maturation Phase: Maximal cell wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications
explanation: Three sequential anatomical zones/phases of cellular growth behind a growing apex.

bullets: Lt: Length at time 't' | L0: Length at time 'zero' | r: Growth rate/elongation per unit time
Division Pattern: Following mitotic division, only ONE daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates (e.g., root elongation)
explanation: Mathematical representation of constant growth rate resulting in a straight linear graph.

bullets: Equation: W1 = W0 * e^(rt) (W1=final size, W0=initial size, r=relative growth rate)
Phases: Lag phase → Log/Exponential phase → Stationary phase
Graph: Classic Sigmoid (S-shaped) curve characteristic of all living organisms in natural environments
explanation: Exponential cell multiplication where both daughter cells retain capacity to divide.

mnemonic: Diff = Mature, Dediff = Regain Division, Rediff = Remature
bullets: Differentiation: Meristematic cell matures to perform specific function (e.g., tracheary element)
Dedifferentiation: Differentiated cell regains division capacity (e.g., Interfascicular cambium, Cork cambium)
Redifferentiation: Dedifferentiated meristem loses division capacity to mature again (e.g., Secondary xylem/phloem, Cork)
explanation: Dynamic developmental pathways of plant cells regaining and losing meristematic activity.

mnemonic: Cotton Coriander Larkspur Development, Buttercup Environment
bullets: Plasticity: Ability of plants to follow different pathways in response to environment or life phases
Developmental Plasticity: Cotton, Coriander, Larkspur (juvenile vs adult leaf shapes differ)
Environmental Plasticity: Buttercup (Ranunculus) (terrestrial vs aquatic leaf shapes differ)
explanation: Morphological flexibility in leaf structure adaptation across phases or habitats. Chapter 13: Plant Growth and Development (30 Mnemonics) 	Page 1

topic: Five Classes of Plant Growth Regulators (PGRs)
mnemonic: Promoters = Auxin, GA, Cytokinin | Inhibitors = Ethylene, ABA
bullets: Growth Promoters: Auxins, Gibberellins (GA), Cytokinins (cell division, growth, pattern formation)
Growth Inhibitors: Abscisic Acid (ABA) (stress response, dormancy, inhibition)
Gaseous/Dual Regulator: Ethylene (fits both, but largely inhibitor of growth activities)
explanation: Classification of 5 plant hormones based on physiological growth responses.

mnemonic: Darwin Canary Grass, Went Avena Curvature
bullets: Charles & Francis Darwin: Discovered phototropism in Canary grass (Phalaris) coleoptiles
F.W. Went: Isolated Auxin from tip of oat (Avena sativa) coleoptiles using agar block
explanation: Key historical experiments leading to the discovery and isolation of IAA.

bullets: Natural Auxins: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), Indole butyric acid (IBA)
Synthetic Auxins: Naphthalene acetic acid (NAA), 2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D)
explanation: Chemical categorization of naturally produced vs artificially synthesized auxins.

bullets: Apical Dominance: Growing apical bud inhibits lateral axillary buds (decapitation promotes branching)
Root Initiation: Used in stem cuttings for plant propagation
Parthenocarpy: Induces seedless fruits in Tomatoes
Selective Weedicide: 2,4-D kills dicotyledonous weeds while sparing monocots
